source_title: Medicine Lodge treaty Art. 12; Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock
source_quote: Four hundred and fifty-six male adults therefore constituted more than three fourths of the certified number
corrected_summary: The 1865 reserve was cut in 1867 to the Medicine Lodge reservation; Art. 12 required three-fourths of adult men to sign any cession. The Jerome commission certified 456 signers out of 562 adult men, which it counted as more than three-fourths; the tribes said their assent was obtained by misrepresentation and that three-fourths had not assented. Congress ratified a changed agreement in 1900 and Lone Wolf upheld Congress's power to do so. The three-fourths shortfall is the tribes' allegation, not a finding.
notes: Lone Wolf gives about 2,150,000 acres of surplus farming and grazing land after excluding 350,000 mountainous acres; the 2.99 million figure was not found. Art. 12 quote matches 15 Stat. 581 ("signed by at least three fourths of all the adult male Indians occupying the same"). Counterfeit-signature claim not checked.

source_title: Fort Wise Feb. 18, 1861; Little Arkansas Oct. 14, 1865 and Senate amendment
source_quote: shall designate for said tribes a reservation, no part of which shall be within the State of Kansas
corrected_summary: Fort Wise ceded most of the 1851 territory and reserved a tract between the Sandy Fork and the Arkansas. The 1865 treaty ceded that reserve and set apart a new one between the Arkansas and Cimarron (partly in Kansas). The Senate amended it on May 22, 1866 so that no part could be in Kansas or on other tribes' land without consent; the chiefs assented Nov. 10 and 19, 1866, and no such reservation was ever designated. The Senate also struck the words naming Col. J. M. Chivington from Art. 6.
notes: The quoted phrase is Senate amendment text, not the original treaty. Sand Creek reparations clause is in 14 Stat. 703 Art. 6.

source_title: Traverse des Sioux and Mendota treaties with Senate amendments; Mdewakanton treaty 1858
source_quote: Strike out the third article of the treaty and add the following
corrected_summary: On June 23, 1852 the Senate struck Art. 3 of each treaty (the reserve of about ten miles on each side of the Minnesota River) and substituted ten cents an acre plus tracts to be chosen by the President. The bands assented on Sept. 8, 1852 (Traverse des Sioux) and Sept. 4, 1852 (Mendota). The President let them "locate for the time being" on the struck reserve, and the 1858 treaties put the north-side land to the Senate. That cash and goods were withheld to force assent is a characterization that needs a named source (e.g., MNHS).
notes: 1858 quote from 12 Stat. 1031: "the President so far varied the conditions of said Senate amendment, as to permit said band* to locate for the time being, upon the tract originally reserved".

source_title: Martin Van Buren, Special Message to the Senate, Jan. 13, 1840 (American Presidency Project); Case of the Seneca Indians (1840)
source_quote: it appeared that 41 signatures of chiefs, including 6 out of the 8 sachems of the nation, had been affixed to the treaty
corrected_summary: The Senate amended the treaty (June 11, 1838) and required each tribe to assent in council. Van Buren reported only 16 Seneca chiefs signed in council and 41 signatures in all, against 74 to 80 or more chiefs; he said the condition had not been met and that improper means had been used, and a Senate committee found bribery clearly shown in at least one case. The Senate ratified anyway and the treaty was proclaimed Apr. 4, 1840. The Society of Friends' 1840 Case of the Seneca Indians counts 16, later 31, of 81 chiefs. The quoted "forty-two out of eighty-one" was not found.
notes: Fellows v. Blacksmith not checked. Fraud and bribery characterization: Van Buren ("improper means have been employed") and the Senate committee report quoted in his message.

source_title: Box Elder treaty July 30, 1863 with Senate amendment; Fort Bridger treaty July 2, 1863 (Kappler)
source_quote: than existed in them upon the acquisition of said territories from Mexico by the laws thereof
corrected_summary: The Senate added a clause that the treaty admitted no greater Indian title than existed under Mexican law (Box Elder new Art. 5; Fort Bridger Art. 7). The bands assented: Box Elder on Nov. 18, 1864 (proclaimed Jan. 17, 1865); Fort Bridger in 1865 (proclaimed June 7, 1869). So this is amended with later assent, not amended without consent; the category SENATE_AMENDED_NO_CONSENT overstates it.
corrected_instrument_cite: 13 Stat. 663 (Box Elder); 18 Stat. 685 (Fort Bridger 1863, per Kappler margin)
notes: Fort Bridger assent day is OCR-garbled in Kappler ("Aug. 31?, 1865"). Ruby Valley not checked.

source_title: Little Arkansas treaty Oct. 14, 1865 with Senate amendments and assent
source_quote: they did, on the tenth day of November, one thousand eight hundred and sixty-six, on behalf of their respective tribes, give their free and voluntary assent to said amendments
corrected_summary: The Senate (May 22, 1866) required that the reservation be outside Kansas and off other tribes' land without their consent, struck the words naming Chivington from Art. 6, and replaced Art. 9 with "all former treaties are hereby abrogated". The chiefs assented Nov. 10 and 19, 1866; proclaimed Feb. 2, 1867. No reservation was designated before Medicine Lodge (1867). This is amended with recorded assent, not without consent.

corrected_summary: The 1889 act divided the Great Sioux Reservation into six reservations and opened the rest, effective only on three-fourths consent under Fort Laramie Art. 12, proven to the President within a year. The acreage (about 9 million) and the Crook Commission's promises, threats and the ration cut were not verified here; the duress label needs a named source.
